title.en: How LLMs Choose Words: Greedy, Temperature & Top-K Decoding

description.en: An LLM outputs probabilities, not words. The decoding strategy — greedy, temperature, top-k — turns those numbers into text, and it's the knob behind 'creative' vs 'precise'. Build the greedy and top-k pickers yourself.

story_variants.en:
## The Model Doesn't Pick a Word. You Do.

"People think an LLM 'says' the next word," Vaathiyaar smiles. "It doesn't. It hands you a **probability for every word in its vocabulary** and steps back. The **decoding strategy** — the code that turns those numbers into an actual choice — is *yours*. It's the difference between a model that's boringly deterministic and one that's wildly creative."

### The Three Everyday Strategies

- **Greedy:** always pick the single highest-probability token. Fast, repeatable, but can get stuck in loops ("the the the"). Great for code and extraction.
- **Temperature:** flatten or sharpen the probabilities before choosing. High temperature = more surprising; low = more focused. It's the "creativity dial."
- **Top-k:** only consider the k most likely tokens, then choose among them. Cuts off the long tail of nonsense while keeping some variety.

```
logits = [1.0, 3.0, 2.0, 0.5]   # one score per vocab token
greedy -> index 1               # highest score wins
top_2  -> indices {1, 2}        # the two best are eligible
```

### Why This Is the Most Practical Thing You'll Learn

Every "temperature" slider, every "make it more creative," every reproducible eval run — all of it is decoding. Understand greedy and top-k and you can explain *why* an LLM repeated itself, or went off the rails, in one sentence.

> **Vaathiyaar's rule:** if output is too random, lower temperature or k. If it's too repetitive, raise them. You are not at the model's mercy — you hold the decoder.

Today you implement `greedy(logits)` (the index of the max) and see decoding from the inside.

uth_example:
import math
import random

vocab = ["pizza", "pasta", "salad", "soup", "cake"]
logits = [3.2, 2.9, 1.0, 0.5, -1.0]

greedy = vocab[max(range(len(logits)), key=lambda i: logits[i])]

def probs(T):
    exps = [math.exp(x / T) for x in logits]
    return [round(e / sum(exps), 3) for e in exps]

top_k = sorted(range(len(logits)), key=lambda i: logits[i], reverse=True)[:2]
rng = random.Random(7)                      # fixed seed: same "random" pick every run
sampled = rng.choices([vocab[i] for i in top_k], weights=[probs(1.0)[i] for i in top_k])[0]

print("greedy:", greedy)
print("T=0.5:", probs(0.5), "| T=2:", probs(2.0))
print("top-2 candidates:", [vocab[i] for i in top_k], "-> sampled:", sampled)

under_the_hood.summary: At each step the model outputs a logit for every vocabulary token; the decoding strategy picks one, either the maximum (greedy) or a random draw from a softmax after dividing logits by a temperature and keeping only the top-k tokens.

steps.title: The model hands you scores
steps.body: For a 4-token toy vocabulary the logits might be [1.0, 3.0, 2.0, 0.5]. The model's job ends here; choosing a token is the decoder's job, and different choices give different text from the same model.

steps.title: Greedy: take the maximum
steps.body: argmax picks token 1 every time. Output is deterministic and good for extraction or code, but long greedy outputs can fall into loops because the same context keeps producing the same choice.

steps.title: Temperature reshapes the odds
steps.body: Divide logits by T before softmax. T < 1 sharpens toward the top token, T > 1 flattens so unlikely tokens get chosen more often, and T approaching 0 becomes greedy.

steps.title: Top-k cuts the tail
steps.body: Keep only the k highest logits and set the rest to -inf. With k = 2, only tokens 1 and 2 are eligible; softmax over [3.0, 2.0] gives [0.731, 0.269], and the draw happens between those two only.

steps.title: Draw and repeat
steps.body: A random number picks a token according to those probabilities; it is appended and the model runs again. Top-p (nucleus) sampling works the same way but keeps the smallest set of tokens whose probabilities sum to p.

under_the_hood.takeaway: The model proposes; the decoder disposes. Greedy, temperature and top-k are three small transformations of one score vector, and they decide how predictable the text is.
